use.how: Describes things you can see that have many bright colours, as an attribute or predicate: 五颜六色的气球 / 花园里五颜六色的。

near.diff: 五花八门 is about many different kinds or varieties; 五颜六色 is only about many visible colours.

cue: A children's party table is covered with red, yellow, green and blue balloons and sweets. How do you describe it?

ctx.s: 孩子们手里拿着{五颜六色}的气球。
ctx.en: The children are holding balloons of every colour.

ctx.s: 秋天到了，山上的树叶变得{五颜六色}，特别好看。
ctx.en: Autumn has come, and the leaves on the hills have turned all sorts of colours; it's beautiful.

ctx.s: 这幅画{五颜六色}的，是你女儿画的吗？
ctx.en: This picture is so colourful. Did your daughter paint it?

ctx.s: 市场里摆满了{五颜六色}的水果和蔬菜。
ctx.en: The market is full of brightly coloured fruit and vegetables.

ctx.s: 她用{五颜六色}的便利贴把学习计划贴满了一面墙。
ctx.en: She covered a whole wall with her study plan on sticky notes of every colour.

ctx.s: 节日的晚上，{五颜六色}的烟花照亮了整个城市。
ctx.en: On the night of the festival, multicoloured fireworks lit up the whole city.

bad.s: 这家书店的书{五颜六色}，什么类型都有。
bad.en: (meant: the bookshop has books of every kind)
bad.why: It describes colours you can see, not a variety of types. For many kinds of things, use the idiom for a dazzling variety (wu hua ba men).

bad.s: 今天的天空{五颜六色}，蓝得发亮。
bad.en: (meant: the sky is a brilliant blue today)
bad.why: It means many different colours at once; a sky of one brilliant blue is not multicoloured.

mean: not knowing whether to laugh or cry
lit: unable to cry and unable to laugh

use.how: Said about something absurd that is annoying and funny at once, often 让人哭笑不得 or 我听了哭笑不得。

near.diff: 莫名其妙 means baffling, with no understandable reason; 哭笑不得 is your reaction to something absurd that is both funny and exasperating.

cue: You asked your little son to wash the car. He washed it with your expensive shampoo and now proudly wants praise.

ctx.s: 他在作文里写“我的爸爸是一只猫”，老师看了{哭笑不得}。
ctx.en: He wrote 'My dad is a cat' in his essay, and the teacher didn't know whether to laugh or cry.

ctx.s: 我让儿子帮我买盐，他买回来一袋糖，真让人{哭笑不得}。
ctx.en: I asked my son to buy salt and he came back with a bag of sugar. I didn't know whether to laugh or cry.

ctx.s: 导航把我们带进了一条死胡同，还说“您已到达目的地”，车里的人都{哭笑不得}。
ctx.en: The satnav led us into a dead end and announced 'You have arrived at your destination'; everyone in the car didn't know whether to laugh or cry.

ctx.s: “狗把你的作业吃了？”“是啊，老师听了这个理由也{哭笑不得}。”
ctx.en: "The dog ate your homework?" "Yes, and when the teacher heard that excuse she didn't know whether to laugh or cry either."

ctx.s: 翻译软件把菜名翻得乱七八糟，外国客人看着菜单{哭笑不得}。
ctx.en: The translation app made a mess of the dish names, and the foreign guests looked at the menu half amused, half exasperated.

ctx.s: 公司为了省电，规定晚上加班不许开空调，员工们对这条规定{哭笑不得}。
ctx.en: To save electricity the company banned air conditioning during evening overtime; the staff didn't know whether to laugh or cry at the rule.

bad.s: 听说奶奶去世了，他{哭笑不得}。
bad.en: (meant: hearing his grandmother had died, he was overwhelmed)
bad.why: It reacts to something absurd and a little funny; using it for real grief sounds flippant and wrong.

bad.s: 收到录取通知书，她高兴得{哭笑不得}。
bad.en: (meant: she was so happy she laughed and cried at once)
bad.why: It implies exasperation at something ridiculous, not pure joy. Tears of happiness call for a different expression.

lit: wiped dry and clean: not a trace left

use.how: A complement after verb + 得: 忘得一干二净, 吃得一干二净, 推得一干二净. Stresses that nothing at all is left.

near.diff: 一清二楚 means knowing or seeing something very clearly; 一干二净 means nothing is left, so 忘得一干二净 is the opposite of 记得一清二楚.

cue: You studied a list of words last night, and this morning you can't recall a single one. How thoroughly did you forget them?

ctx.s: 一盘饺子被孩子们吃得{一干二净}。
ctx.en: The children ate the whole plate of dumplings; not one was left.

ctx.s: 昨天学的单词，我今天就忘得{一干二净}了。
ctx.en: The words I learned yesterday, I've completely forgotten today.

ctx.s: 你怎么把我们的约会忘得{一干二净}？
ctx.en: How could you completely forget our date?

ctx.s: 出了问题以后，他把责任推得{一干二净}。
ctx.en: When things went wrong, he pushed off every bit of the responsibility.

ctx.s: 小偷把店里值钱的东西偷得{一干二净}。
ctx.en: The thief took every last valuable thing in the shop.

ctx.s: 搬走之前，她把旧房子打扫得{一干二净}才交了钥匙。
ctx.en: Before moving out, she cleaned the old flat spotless and only then handed back the keys.

bad.s: 他对这件事知道得{一干二净}。
bad.en: (meant: he knows all about this matter)
bad.why: It means nothing is left, so it cannot express thorough knowledge. Use 'know very clearly' (yi qing er chu) instead.

bad.s: 他是一个{一干二净}的人。
bad.en: (meant: he is a neat, tidy person)
bad.why: It is a degree complement after a verb (swept spotlessly clean), not a description of a person's tidiness.

mean: to think one is always right
lit: to take oneself to be right

story.text: In the Mencius, Mencius explains why Confucius despised the 'village worthy': a man whom everyone in his village likes, who seems loyal and honest but simply goes along with the world. Everyone is pleased with him and he thinks himself right, yet he cannot enter the Way of the sage kings Yao and Shun. That is why Confucius called such people thieves of virtue.

use.how: A predicate or attribute criticising someone who will not listen to others: 他太自以为是了 / 自以为是的人; also adverbial 自以为是地。

near.diff: 不懂装懂 is pretending to know what you don't; 自以为是 is sincerely believing you are right and ignoring others.

cue: Your teammate brushes off every suggestion, insists his plan is the only correct one, and is surprised when it fails.

ctx.s: 他太{自以为是}了，从来不听别人的建议。
ctx.en: He is far too sure he's right; he never listens to anyone's advice.

ctx.s: 别那么{自以为是}，你也可能会错。
ctx.en: Don't be so sure of yourself; you could be wrong too.

ctx.s: 新来的经理很{自以为是}，开会时总是打断大家。
ctx.en: The new manager thinks he's always right and keeps interrupting everyone in meetings.

ctx.s: 他总是{自以为是}地替别人做决定，结果谁都不满意。
ctx.en: He always decides things for other people, sure he knows best, and in the end nobody is happy.

ctx.s: 年轻时我有点{自以为是}，后来吃了亏才明白要多听别人的。
ctx.en: When I was young I was rather sure I was always right; only after paying for it did I learn to listen to others.

ctx.s: 这篇评论写得很{自以为是}，好像只有作者的看法才是对的。
ctx.en: This review is written very self-righteously, as if only the author's view could be correct.

bad.s: 她很{自以为是}，所以面试表现得很好。
bad.en: (meant: she is self-confident, so her interview went well)
bad.why: It criticises arrogance and refusal to listen; it is never praise for healthy self-confidence.

bad.s: 我{自以为是}你的看法。
bad.en: (meant: I think your view is right)
bad.why: It is about oneself thinking one is right and takes no object; to agree with someone else's view, say you think their view is right.

story.text: The phrase comes from the Great Learning, which argues that cultivating oneself depends on setting the mind right: when the mind is not present, one looks but does not see, listens but does not hear, and eats without knowing the taste of the food.

use.how: A predicate or adverbial (心不在焉地) about someone whose attention is elsewhere at the moment, often mildly critical: 上课心不在焉。

near.diff: 粗心大意 is a careless habit that causes mistakes; 心不在焉 is a passing state of having your mind on something else.

cue: Your friend keeps stirring her coffee and staring out of the window, answering you with 'mm' without hearing a word.

ctx.s: 上课的时候，他一直{心不在焉}，老师叫了他两次都没听见。
ctx.en: All through the lesson his mind was somewhere else; the teacher called his name twice and he didn't hear.

ctx.s: 你今天怎么{心不在焉}的？有什么心事吗？
ctx.en: Why are you so distracted today? Is something on your mind?

ctx.s: 她{心不在焉}地搅着咖啡，眼睛一直看着窗外。
ctx.en: She absent-mindedly stirred her coffee, her eyes fixed on the window.

ctx.s: 开会时小王{心不在焉}，老板问他问题，他连问的是什么都不知道。
ctx.en: Xiao Wang's mind was elsewhere in the meeting; when the boss asked him something, he didn't even know what the question was.

ctx.s: 我跟他说了半天，他只是{心不在焉}地“嗯”了几声。
ctx.en: I talked to him for ages, and he just went 'mm' a few times without really listening.

ctx.s: 比赛前一天晚上，他看书看得{心不在焉}，满脑子都是明天的比赛。
ctx.en: The night before the match he read without taking anything in; all he could think of was the game.

bad.s: 我给他打电话，他{心不在焉}，家里没人。
bad.en: (meant: I phoned him but he wasn't at home)
bad.why: It means the mind is elsewhere while the person is present; it says nothing about being physically absent.

bad.s: 度假的时候，我{心不在焉}，什么烦恼都没有。
bad.en: (meant: on holiday I was carefree)
bad.why: It means distracted and inattentive, not relaxed. For being carefree, use a different idiom (wu you wu lv).

mean: half-hearted; unable to commit to one thing

use.how: A predicate or adverbial criticising someone who keeps switching and won't commit: 做事三心二意 / 别三心二意了。Also used of fickleness in love.

near.diff: 一心一意 is its opposite: wholehearted devotion to one thing.

cue: A student practises piano for ten minutes, switches to drawing, then picks up the guitar, and finishes none of them.

ctx.s: 学习的时候不能{三心二意}。
ctx.en: When you study, you can't keep half your mind on other things.

ctx.s: 他做作业总是{三心二意}，一会儿看手机，一会儿吃零食。
ctx.en: He never sticks to his homework: one minute he's on his phone, the next he's snacking.

ctx.s: 你一会儿想学吉他，一会儿想学画画，再这样{三心二意}，什么都学不好。
ctx.en: One minute you want to learn guitar, the next painting; if you keep chopping and changing like this, you'll never master anything.

ctx.s: 她一年换了好几个专业，父母说她太{三心二意}了。
ctx.en: She changed her major several times in one year, and her parents said she couldn't commit to anything.

ctx.s: 对感情{三心二意}的人，很难得到别人的信任。
ctx.en: People who are fickle in love find it hard to win others' trust.

ctx.s: “我还是想学画画……”“别{三心二意}了，选一个就坚持下去。”
ctx.en: "Actually I'd rather learn painting..." "Stop flitting about. Pick one and stick with it."

bad.s: 他{三心二意}，一次能做三件事。
bad.en: (meant: he is good at multitasking)
bad.why: It criticises a lack of commitment; it is never praise for doing several things at once.

bad.s: 做这个决定之前，我{三心二意}地考虑了很久。
bad.en: (meant: I thought it over carefully from every angle)
bad.why: It means half-hearted and fickle, not careful thought. For careful deliberation use 'think deeply' (shen si shu lv).

lit: seven going up and eight going down

use.how: Almost always about the heart: 心里七上八下(的). Describes nervous unease while waiting for an uncertain outcome.

near.diff: 提心吊胆 is fearing danger over a period of time; 七上八下 is the jumpy, unsettled feeling while you wait to find out how something turned out.

cue: You sat the most important exam of your life last week, and the results come out tomorrow morning. How does your heart feel tonight?

ctx.s: 等考试成绩的时候，我心里{七上八下}的。
ctx.en: While I was waiting for my exam results, my stomach was in knots.

ctx.s: 第一次上台演讲，他心里{七上八下}，手都在发抖。
ctx.en: Giving his first speech on stage, he was so jittery that his hands shook.

ctx.s: 儿子去参加篮球队的选拔，妈妈在家等消息，心里{七上八下}的。
ctx.en: Her son had gone to the basketball team trials, and his mother waited at home for news, her heart all of a flutter.

ctx.s: 面试结束后，她心里一直{七上八下}的，不知道能不能被录取。
ctx.en: After the interview she was on edge the whole time, not knowing whether she'd be hired.

ctx.s: “医生怎么还不出来？”“别急，我心里也{七上八下}的。”
ctx.en: "Why hasn't the doctor come out yet?" "Hang on, I'm on edge too."

ctx.s: 公司要裁员，名单明天公布，办公室里每个人心里都{七上八下}。
ctx.en: The company is cutting jobs and the list comes out tomorrow; everyone in the office feels uneasy.

bad.s: 我们爬山爬得{七上八下}，累死了。
bad.en: (meant: we climbed up and down the hills all day)
bad.why: It describes an anxious state of mind, not physical movement up and down.

bad.s: 收到礼物，她心里{七上八下}，开心极了。
bad.en: (meant: she was thrilled to get the present)
bad.why: It is anxiety and unease, not happy excitement.

lit: hands busy and feet in a muddle

use.how: A predicate or adverbial (手忙脚乱地) for clumsy, disorganised hurry when caught unprepared: 客人一来，她就手忙脚乱。

near.diff: 不可开交 stresses having too much to do to get away; 手忙脚乱 stresses flustered, clumsy disorder.
惊慌失措 is panic from fear or shock; 手忙脚乱 is a disorganised rush, often with no fear at all.

cue: Guests ring the doorbell early; you are still dropping dishes and pulling on mismatched socks as you tidy up.

ctx.s: 客人突然来了，妈妈{手忙脚乱}地收拾房间。
ctx.en: Guests turned up unexpectedly, and Mum rushed around tidying the room in a fluster.

ctx.s: 第一次给宝宝换尿布，爸爸{手忙脚乱}的。
ctx.en: Changing the baby's nappy for the first time, Dad was all fingers and thumbs.

ctx.s: 闹钟没响，我早上{手忙脚乱}，连袜子都穿反了。
ctx.en: My alarm didn't go off, and in the morning rush I even put my socks on inside out.

ctx.s: 餐厅一下子来了很多客人，新来的服务员{手忙脚乱}，把菜送错了桌。
ctx.en: A crowd of customers arrived at once; the new waiter got flustered and took dishes to the wrong table.

ctx.s: “快点，车要开了！”“别催我，越催我越{手忙脚乱}。”
ctx.en: "Hurry up, the bus is leaving!" "Stop rushing me, the more you rush me the more flustered I get."

ctx.s: 只要提前准备好材料，到时候就不会{手忙脚乱}了。
ctx.en: As long as you get the materials ready in advance, you won't be scrambling when the time comes.

bad.s: 他工作很{手忙脚乱}，但每件事都安排得井井有条。
bad.en: (meant: he is very busy but well organised)
bad.why: It means flustered and disorganised, so it contradicts 'well organised'. To say simply busy, just say 'very busy'.

bad.s: 他摔倒以后{手忙脚乱}，腿疼得走不了路。
bad.en: (meant: after falling, his arms and legs hurt)
bad.why: It describes a frantic rush, not injured hands and feet.

lit: so pressed that one cannot wait

use.how: Usually an adverbial before the action someone is eager to do: 迫不及待地打开 / 迫不及待想看; can also stand as a predicate: 我已经迫不及待了。

near.diff: 争分夺秒 is racing against the clock to finish in time; 迫不及待 is eagerness to start something right now.

cue: A parcel you have waited a month for finally arrives, and you tear it open right there at the front door.

ctx.s: 一放学，孩子们就{迫不及待}地跑出了教室。
ctx.en: As soon as school was out, the children dashed out of the classroom.

ctx.s: 收到快递，她{迫不及待}地打开了盒子。
ctx.en: When the parcel arrived, she couldn't wait to open the box.

ctx.s: 新手机一上市，他就{迫不及待}地买了一部。
ctx.en: The moment the new phone came out, he rushed to buy one.

ctx.s: “电影什么时候上映？”“下个月，我已经{迫不及待}了！”
ctx.en: "When does the film come out?" "Next month. I can't wait!"

ctx.s: 他还没听完问题，就{迫不及待}地开始回答。
ctx.en: He started answering before he'd even heard the whole question.

ctx.s: 天气刚暖和一点，公园里的花就{迫不及待}地开了。
ctx.en: The weather had barely warmed up when the flowers in the park eagerly burst into bloom.

bad.s: 时间{迫不及待}，我们必须马上出发。
bad.en: (meant: time is pressing, we must leave now)
bad.why: It describes a person's eagerness, not urgent time. To say time is pressing, say that time is tight.

bad.s: 一听说要打针，孩子就{迫不及待}地哭了起来。
bad.en: (meant: as soon as he heard about the injection, the child burst into tears)
bad.why: It means eager to do something you want to do; it cannot describe an instant reaction of fear or dread.

use.how: Usually an adverbial (不慌不忙地 + verb) or predicate, for someone who acts calmly when others would rush: 他不慌不忙地回答。

near.diff: 心平气和 is calm in temper, not angry; 不慌不忙 is calm in pace, not rushing under pressure.

cue: The fire alarm goes off and everyone runs, but one teacher calmly lines up the children and walks them out.

ctx.s: 他{不慌不忙}地喝完茶才出门。
ctx.en: He took his time finishing his tea before he left.

ctx.s: 警报响了，老师{不慌不忙}地带着学生走出教学楼。
ctx.en: The alarm went off, and the teacher calmly led the students out of the building.

ctx.s: 面对记者的问题，她{不慌不忙}，一个一个地回答。
ctx.en: Faced with the reporters' questions, she kept her composure and answered them one by one.

ctx.s: 大家都急得团团转，只有他{不慌不忙}的，把东西一件件装进箱子。
ctx.en: Everyone was rushing around in a panic; only he stayed unhurried, packing things into the box one by one.

ctx.s: “车快开了，你怎么还{不慌不忙}的？”“别担心，还有十分钟呢。”
ctx.en: "The train's about to leave, why are you still dawdling?" "Relax, there are still ten minutes."

ctx.s: 比赛只剩最后一分钟，他仍然{不慌不忙}地运球，找准机会投进了一球。
ctx.en: With one minute left in the game, he kept dribbling calmly, picked his moment and scored.

bad.s: 这家公司这几年发展得{不慌不忙}，越来越好。
bad.en: (meant: the company has grown steadily in recent years)
bad.why: It describes how a person acts under time pressure, not the steady growth of a company. Say it grew steadily.

bad.s: 他脾气特别好，跟家人从来{不慌不忙}，没吵过一次架。
bad.en: (meant: he is very good-tempered and has never once quarrelled with his family)
bad.why: It is about pace and composure, not temper. For someone who never gets angry, use 'calm and even-tempered'.
